Bankart lesions do not heal conservatively and need to be surgically repaired to decrease the likelihood of redislocation. A
Conservative treatment with immobilization and physical therapy does not reduce high redislocation rates. A

In individuals older than 40 years, redislocation rates are much lower. Therefore, nonsurgical treatment with immobilization in a sling long enough to relieve symptoms followed by physical therapy is appropriate. A

background.definition: Shoulder dislocation is defined as complete loss of the humeral articulation with the glenoid fossa. Classification is based on (1) direction of displacement of humeral head (anterior, posterior, inferior), (2) frequency (acute, recurrent, chronic), and (3) etiology (traumatic or spontaneous).

list.listitem: Shoulder dislocations account for more than 50% of major joint dislocations, constituting the most common musculoskeletal injury seen in the emergency department.
Anterior glenohumeral instability affects just under 2% of the general population of which dislocations are a subset.

Anterior dislocations account for up to 97% of all shoulder dislocations, with posterior dislocations acocunting for 2-4%, and inferior dislocations (luxatio erecta), the most uncommon type, accounting for less that 1%.
Traumatic first time anterior shoulder dislocation peak incidence in men aged 16-20 years. Peak incidence in women aged 61 to 70 years.
The shoulder joint is an unstable joint due to a shallow glenoid that only articulates with a small part of the humeral head.

Anterior dislocation: usually indirect levering of the humeral head anteriorly with the shoulder positioned in some combination of abduction, hyperextension, and external rotation. It can also occur as a result of a fall on outstretched hand or a direct blow to shoulder with the force directed anteriorly.

Posterior dislocation: A systematic review identified 182 patients with posterior glenohumeral dislocation and found that seizures were associated with 38%. Other reasons included falls, motor vehicle accidents, electric shock, and iatrogenic reasons.
Inferior dislocation: hyperabduction injury at shoulder.

The joint capsule and its thickenings, called glenohumeral ligaments, provide soft tissue support to the glenohumeral joint. The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) is an important restraint for anterior dislocations.

A Bankart lesion is a detachment of the IGHL-labral complex from the anterior glenoid rim, and it appears to be associated with more than 95% first-time posttraumatic anterior dislocations in young individuals.
The Bankart lesion is associated with recurrent anterior dislocations unless surgically repaired.
In individuals more than 40 years old, tears of the subscapularis and the anterior capsule from the lesser tubercle are associated with anterior dislocations, as shown in cadaveric studies.

With poterior dislocations, higher risk of fractures of the surgical neck or tuberostiy, reverse Hill-Sachs lesions, and labral or rotator cuff injuries. With inferior dislocations, highest incidence of injury to axillary nerve and artery.
The diagnosis of shoulder dislocation is usually obvious from history and physical examination. C
Prereduction radiographs can be limited to individuals with first-time dislocation, age more than 40 years, and history of trauma. B
At least two orthogonal radiographs should be obtained to confirm direction of dislocation: anteroposterior along with a lateral (transcapular) or axillary view. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Anterior versus posterior versus inferior dislocation
Differential.Differential_Features: Typical injury, clinical presentation, plain films
Fall on shoulder or injury to clavicle with heavy object, deformity, bump at fracture
History of fall, swelling, pain, bruising around upper arm or shoulder, plain films
Fall onto the tip of the shoulder, pain over the AC joint, pain on lifting arm, arm held in adduction
Fall on shoulder or other mechanism of injury involving rotator cuff muscles

list.listitem: Anterior dislocation: Patient may give history of the usual mechanism of injury (see Causes). Patients may also report a popping sensation, sudden onset of pain with decreased range of motion, or the sensation of the joint rolling out of the socket. On physical examination, there is anterior fullness caused by the displaced humeral head. The affected shoulder is often held in slight abduction, external rotation, cradling the forearm with the unaffected arm. History of a recent dislocation that has been reduced should be sought since the physical examination findings above will be absent in that case.

Among 60 consecutive patients confirmed to have anterior shoulder instability by MRI, three physical examination tests were useful in diagnosis, including: the release test, the relocation test (96.7% sensitive) and the the anterior drawer test (92.7% specific).

In order to replicate these tests do the following: Apprehension test: Have the patient lay supine with the arm in 90° abduction, the elbow in 90° flexion, and with maximum external rotation; apply anterior, external rotatory force. A positive test is when the patient experiences apprehension with the maneuver; immediately after this test do the relocation test. Relocation test: Perform the relocation test with the patient in the position that evoked apprehension, depress the humeral head in the posterior direction. If the patients experiences relief from "apprehension" and they can tolerate maximal external rotation then the test is positive. Anterior release test: The anterior release test is carried out immediately after the relocation test. The examiner releases the pressure on the humeral heal, and a positive test is when the patient experiences "apprehension." Anterior drawer test: The anterior drawer test is when the examiner grasps the humerus and draws it out anteriorly after stabilizing the scapula. A positive test is when the patient experiences "apprehension" or the humeral head moves anteriorly.

Posterior dislocation: Patient may have history of a seizure, electric shock, or trauma. Presentation might be subtle, and physical examination findings might be limited to posterior joint line tenderness. Active and passive range of motion might be normal.
Inferior dislocation: Patient presents with shoulder pain, inability to move affected shoulder, and arm is fixed in an elevated or abducted position.

Radiographs help diagnose direction of dislocation and associated fractures, and confirm reduction of dislocation. It is controversial whether prereduction x-rays should be done in every case of shoulder dislocation.

One recent study showed that x-rays limited to individuals with any of the following first-time dislocation were 98% sensitive for detecting associated fractures: age more than 40 years and history of significant trauma such as a fall greater than one flight of stairs, a fight/assault episode, or a motor vehicle crash.

It is generally accepted that at least two orthogonal radiographs should be obtained to confirm the direction of dislocation: anteroposterior along with a lateral (transcapular) or axillary view. However, no good evidence exists to support this practice.
Appropriate plain films will identify most dislocations, so MRI is not routinely recommended.

In a prospective observational study of 103 patients (mean age 40) with possible shoulder dislocation, point-of-care ultrasound to detect should dislocation (before radiographic studies) was 100% sensitive and specific, and 100% sensitive and 84% specific for excluding shoulder fracture.

A systematic review found that point of care ultrasound (POCUS) is nearly 100% sensitive and specific for diagnosing shoulder dislocations and associated fractures, based on data from 10 studies involving 1,836 assessments.

The clinical diagnosis of anterior dislocation is fairly obvious. The patient may give history of the usual mechanism of injury. Patient may also present with history of recent dislocation that has already been reduced.

The presentation of posterior dislocation can often be subtle, with prominence of the coracoid process and the arm held in adduction with internal rotation (unable to externaly rotate), but the diagnosis may be missed.

Inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta) are most commonly the result of a forceful hyperabduction of the arm, and often (approximately 60%) present with some degree of neurologic dysfunction (most commonly involving the axillary nerve); arterial injury, presenting with absent or reduced radial pulse, can also occur.

Younger individuals involved in highly demanding physical activity like contact or collision sports should consider having surgical repair of Bankart lesion after an acute first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. A Athletes may have varied ability to return to sport with 20% to 94% of patients returning to their sport after surgical or nonoperative management. Overhead athletes had a lower average return of 45% compared to 55% of athletes fully returning to participate.
Arthroscopic Bankart repair appears to be as good as open repair in preventing recurrent dislocation. A

Individuals older than 40 years, individuals with low levels of activity, and individuals who choose not to have surgery can be immobilized in a sling with or without a postimmobilization exercise program. A
Duration of immobilization should be long enough to relieve symptoms, and this has no effect on redislocation rates. B
Surgical repair of the classic Bankart lesion is now recommended in young athletes (see Table) who have sustained their first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation.

A network meta-analysis of 15 studies concluded that arthroscopic Bankart repair is the best initial treatment option to reduce rates of redisclocation (RR 0.15 compared with internal rotation immobilization).Arthroscopic lavage (RR .47) and external rotation immobilization (RR 0.70) had trends favoring them in terms of redislocation over internal rotation immobilization.
In an RCT with 80 consecutive patients, primary repair in patients between the ages of 15 years and 39 years resulted in fewer subsequent dislocations and improved patient satisfaction.

A meta-analysis of 5 studies (259 patients) aged 15 to 39 years of age with acute anterior dislocations who were treated surgically were less likely to have recurrent instability than those who were treated nonsurgically.
Arthoscopic Bankart repair has been shown to be as effective as open repair in preventing redislocation.

A systematic review of 14 observational studies of revision arthroscopic Bankart repair found relatively high rates of recurrent instability (26%) and low rates to pre-injury level of play in athletes (49%).
Bone block augmentation and grafting is used for patients with shoulder instability, but randomized trials are lacking.

After reduction, the traditional conservative management with sling immobilization followed by an exercise program has been shown to have high redislocation rates of around 50% to 80%, regardless of the position and duration of sling. This is especially true in young, highly physically active athletes.

A meta-analysis of 7 trials (6 RCTs and 1 quasi-RCT) with a total of 704 participants compared immobilization in external rotation vs internal rotation, demonstrating risk ratio (RR) of 0.67 for recurrent dislocation, with very low certainty evidence (confidence interval 0.38-1.1). Further studies are pending and necessary, as current evidence is insufficient to inform the best choice for immobilization position to reduce recurrence

A subsequent systematic review identified 9 studies with 795 patients comparing immobilization in external versus internal rotation following an initial anterior shoulder dislocation. They found better adherence (75% vs 67%, p = 0.01, NNT = 12) and a lower likelihood of recurrent dislocation (22% vs 33%, p = 0.02, NNT = 9) with immobilization in external rotation. There was also a greater likelihood of return to play in athletes (60% vs 43%, p = 0.001, NNT 6).
Rehabilitative exercises after immobilization have not been very effective in preventing dislocation but may improve symptoms.

After a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation and after an initial visit to a physical therapist for education and exercise planning, additional physical therapy up to 4 months shows no significant impact on shoulder instability, disability, or quality of life.

In patients older than 40 years, patients with low levels of activity, and patients who decline surgery, immobilization for a period of time enough to relieve symptoms with or without physical therapy may be considered.

Acute dislocation can be reduced using any of the several described techniques depending on the expertise of the physician: premedication with IV agents, inhaled nitrous oxide, or intraarticular lidocaine.

No clear evidence exists to recommend any particular reduction method over another; scapular manipulation is relatively simple to perform and causes minimal trauma. It can be performed with the patient either seated or lying prone. The affected arm is held in 90° of forward flexion either by an assistant or with a 10-pound weight attached to wrist if prone. The operator pushes the inferior tip of the scapula medially with one hand while the opposite hand stabilizes and rotates the lateral-superior border of the scapula in the inferior direction.
Scapulohumeral distraction technique has been proposed and was similar to the Hippocratic technique in efficacy in a randomized trial.

The reduction can be performed with or without analgesia, depending on level of prereduction pain and anxiety level. If analgesia is chosen, the preferred option is intraarticular 1% lidocaine mixed with 0.25% bupivicaine, usually 10 to 20 cc total volume. Alternatively, an IV benzodiazepine along with an IV narcotic can be used.
A recent Cochrane review concluded that the use of intraarticular lignocaine was as effective and associated with fewer adverse effects than IV analgesia with or without sedation.

Suprascapular nerve block (SNB) was applied under ultrasound guidance was as effective as ketamine intravenously for procedural sedation associated with reductions of shoulder dislocations in the emergency department.

A network meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials (957 patients) compared intravenous sedation (IVS), intraarticular anesthetic injection (IAA), and peripheral nerve block (PNB) for anterior shoulder dislocation reduction. There was little difference in success rates and patient satisfaction among the methods.

If scapular manipulation fails, another relatively atraumatic reduction manuever is the external rotation method. With the patient lying supine with the affected elbow flexed to 90° and the shoulder adducted against the patient's flank, the operator slowly (over 5-10 minutes) externally rotates the shoulder until a reduction is accomplished. This technique can be performed with or without analgesia.
Rarely, nerve (typicaly axillary nerve) and vascular (typically axillary artery) injuries can ocur from reduction attempts, or from recurrent dislocations, most commonly in those over the age of 40.

Outcomes are improved with interprofessional team management of shoulder dislocation injuries, including primary care and emergency physicians, physical therapists, and orthopedic physicians when appropriate.

Younger individuals involved in highly demanding physical activity like contact or collision sports have high redislocation rates of around 50% to 80% if surgical Bankart repair is not done. Rates are lower in persons over 40 years old. A
Studies show that young age at the time of dislocation and high levels of physical activity, such as contact or collision sports, increase likelihood of redislocation. B

In a meta-analysis of 15 studies (N = 22,845), the overall pooled recurrence rate was 21%. However, the corresponding rate for just the prospective studies was 47%. The overall pooled time to recurrence was 10.8 months.
Radiographs are recommended in children since proximal humeral physis might be open and physical fractures need to be ruled out.
